[Supreme Court]{.status .status-case} [568 U.S. 398](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-568/pdf/USREPORTS-568-398.pdf){.cite} [Decided February 26, 2013]{.cite} [5 to 4]{.cite}

**Holding.** No. Their fear that their communications would be collected was too speculative to establish the concrete, imminent injury Article III requires, and their costs to avoid surveillance could not substitute for it.

**Question.** Whether lawyers, journalists, and human rights groups who communicate with people abroad had standing to challenge Section 702 of FISA, which authorizes surveillance targeting non-U.S. persons outside the United States.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the opinion** (official text)

[Opinion: 568 U.S. 398](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-568/pdf/USREPORTS-568-398.pdf){.btn-official}
:::

Background reading: [Wikipedia article on Clapper v. Amnesty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clapper_v._Amnesty_International_USA) (secondary source).

## Why it matters

Clapper made Section 702 very hard to challenge in ordinary court, which leaves oversight largely to the intelligence committees, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, and the periodic reauthorization fights over the [FISA Amendments Act (702)](../statutes/fisa-amendments-2008.qmd) and the [RISAA](../statutes/risaa-2024.qmd). The Court did not reach the program's legality.

## Status

Good law.

## Statutes at issue

- [FISA Amendments Act (702)](../statutes/fisa-amendments-2008.qmd){.subj}. Dismissed a facial challenge to Section 702 for lack of standing, without reaching the merits.

Studied in [Unit 7: Surveillance law](../study/units/surveillance.qmd).
